name: PT Waskita Beton Precast Tbk

frontmatter.title: Waskita Beton Precast — a precast franchise that belongs to its creditors
frontmatter.summary: WSBP makes precast and ready-mix concrete inside the Waskita Karya group. The operating business is real but small and shrinking; the balance sheet is not. Liabilities exceed assets, equity is a deficiency, reported EBITDA is negative once the LK depreciation charge replaces the data pack figure, and the eighth bond coupon has been deferred. We initiate NOT RATED: the DCF equity value is negative, limited liability floors it there, and the shares are suspended.
thesis: The value is decided by the balance sheet, not the business. Liabilities exceed assets by more than the operating business could ever earn, so a shareholder ranks behind creditors who have already restructured once and are now being paid in shares.

Reported profitability is worse than the data shows. The LK depreciation charge is more than double the pack figure, and on the audited numbers EBITDA is negative; the company’s own going-concern note says there is material uncertainty about continuing as a going concern.

WSBP is losing share in a growing market. Nine-month revenue fell while national cement demand grew, and a price war on close to half of national capacity lying idle leaves little room to pass costs through.
Finance cost exceeds gross profit. Even a full recovery to the company’s own margin target does not cover interest, and the funding gap is met by non-payment and conversion rather than new money.

The base case is not a liquidation. Revenue grows with the market and margins recover as the coal and oil decks ease; value is zero because enterprise value never clears net debt, not because we assume the plants stop.

The tail is two-sided but the upside accrues to creditors. A conversion large enough to restore solvency repairs the balance sheet and hands the creditors the shares; it does not repair the enterprise, whose discounted cash flow is negative before any debt.

catalysts.event: Listing of the new shares issued to creditors at the conversion price set in the peace agreement, which fixes the post-placement share base
End of the ninety-day window the company gave itself to pay the deferred eighth bond coupon
Next scheduled bond coupon and the cash-waterfall test under the homologated peace agreement
Full-year results, and whether the auditor repeats the going-concern emphasis

blocks.text: **NOT RATED — valuation view Rp0 on a Rp14 last-traded price that is a suspension sticker, not a market price.** A rating is a twelve-month total-return expectation measured from a price an investor can deal at, and WSBP has no such price: trading has been suspended at the last print, with no executable price to earn a return against [S2]. The house rule is explicit that a suspended line is NOT RATED rather than held, bought or sold on a theoretical return (`fund rules`, ratings: "NOT RATED: suspended / insufficient data"), and the engine enforces it from the exchange status. We publish the work as a valuation view only: no target and no expected return are published for a suspended line, because there is no executable price to measure a return against. This is not a liquidation forecast and not a judgement that precast concrete has no economic use in Indonesia. It is the arithmetic of a balance sheet on which liabilities of 5,247 IDR bn stand against total assets of 2,878 IDR bn at the end of September 2026, leaving an equity deficiency of -2,369 IDR bn and nothing for a residual claimant [S4]. Whatever the operating business is worth, that value accrues to the banks, bondholders and suppliers who have already accepted a restructuring once and are now being paid in new shares.

The operating case is weak but not absurd, and the distinction matters. Nine-month revenue was 1,078 IDR bn, down from the prior year, with gross profit of 130 IDR bn that leaves the company earning a margin in the low teens on a cost base carrying the depreciation of a plant built for far more volume [S4]. Our model has revenue recovering to IDR1,861.1bn by the end of the forecast and the EBITDA loss narrowing from IDR-134.2bn to IDR-28.5bn as coal and oil costs ease along the deck path. It still does not produce a single year of positive free cash flow, and the finance cost alone is IDR468.8bn in that final year.

The engine’s DCF therefore produces an enterprise value of IDR-125.3bn, negative because every forecast year’s free cash flow is negative, and after net debt at the September balance sheet — interest-bearing debt of 3,689 IDR bn less cash of 28.1 IDR bn — and the mandatory convertible bond added back as equity in substance, an unfloored equity value of minus several trillion rupiah, which limited liability floors at zero. EV/EBITDA and P/BV cannot be computed at all: one needs positive EBITDA, the other positive book equity, and WSBP has neither [S5][S4]. The DCF carries the whole valuation not by preference but because it is the only method with a denominator that exists.

Our variant view is about the claim, not the cycle. The market capitalises the shares at IDR771.6bn against liabilities of 5,247 IDR bn [S0][S4]. The only structural upside is a debt conversion, and we have run it rather than asserted it away: converting the whole 3,689 IDR bn of interest-bearing debt at the 50.81 rupiah price set in the peace agreement would issue about seventy-three billion new shares on the 56,959 million already in issue, turn the deficiency into positive book equity of about ten rupiah a share, and leave the enterprise value negative — so the equity is still worth nothing on a cash-flow basis and, on a book basis, less than the last traded price. A write-off large enough to bring liabilities below the value of the assets does not create earning power either. Neither is in the current documents.

The base case is the most probable path, not the most cautious one. Volume tracks the national market after this year’s share loss, price rises with inflation plus partial cost pass-through, gross margin recovers as the coal and oil decks fall, and general and administrative costs stop growing. Nothing in the model assumes the plants are shut, the contracts are cancelled or the assets are sold at a discount. The zero is produced by debt service, and that is the honest reason to own none of this equity.

WSBP manufactures and installs precast concrete products and supplies ready-mix concrete, with construction services attached to the larger projects. The company sits inside the Waskita Karya group: it was incorporated by PT Waskita Karya (Persero) Tbk and remains its listed subsidiary, which determines both the work it wins and the counterparties it is paid by [S5][S2]. Its registered office is in East Jakarta and it employs 676 people, a headcount already cut hard through the restructuring [S0].

The revenue model has two engines. Sales of precast, ready-mix and steel are recognised when control passes to the customer, meaning on delivery to the project site; construction services are recognised on a percentage-of-completion basis, which puts revenue at the mercy of physical progress and of the certification of that progress by the client [S5]. Cost of revenues splits between cost of goods sold and cost of construction services, with goods production the larger block; within goods production, labour and factory overhead dominate, and overhead is where the coal, power and diesel exposure sits [S5].

The customer base is the defining feature of the business and, in our view, its central risk. 1,107 IDR bn of FY2025 revenue came from related parties against total revenue of IDR1,569.6bn, roughly seven tenths of the whole, and related-party receivables are a large share of the trade receivables book [S5]. The company states that its 2026 project pipeline should come predominantly from external parties such as the public works ministry, other state ministries, regional-owned enterprises and private developers, with the balance from Waskita Karya itself [S5]. That is the right direction commercially, but it is a plan rather than a position, and the largest external client in Indonesian construction is also a state entity with its own cash constraints.

Strategy in the documents is a survival plan rather than a growth plan: a new-contract target of 2,600 IDR bn and revenue of 2,100 IDR bn for the year, a gross margin target of about one fifth of revenue, the sale of non-productive fixed assets, a ten per cent cut in general and administrative costs against the original budget, positive EBITDA as the test of any expansion, and full compliance with the homologated peace agreement [S5][S6]. Revenue was already 1,078 IDR bn at the nine-month stage, so the 2,100 IDR bn plan needs a final quarter roughly the size of the entire first nine months — about three times the quarterly run-rate — and the company will miss it by close to a third. Our own IDR1,448.1bn implies a fourth quarter a few per cent above the run-rate, not a collapse. The margin target is roughly what the FY2025 accounts delivered; the nine-month figures show it halving, which is why we model recovery over several years rather than a return to target next year.

On capacity and position, the company states precast production capacity of 3.7 Mt a year [S8]. Against revenue of IDR1,569.6bn and a blended price around one and a half million rupiah a tonne, that capacity is running at roughly a quarter of utilisation, so the fixed-cost absorption problem is structural: the depreciation and the plant overhead are there whether or not the order book is. WSBP is not a cement producer. It buys cement and aggregates and adds formwork, labour and logistics, which makes it a challenger in a fragmented fabrication segment rather than a participant in the national cement oligopoly [S5][S9].

Precast concrete is made in a factory rather than poured on site, which trades flexibility for speed, consistent quality and less waste, and it is the standard solution for toll-road girders, bridges, drainage, retaining walls and marine works. The economics of a precast plant are those of any heavy fabrication business: high fixed cost, a catchment area limited by transport cost, and utilisation as the swing factor in margin. Demand follows the construction cycle with a lag, because the product sits at the front end of a project rather than the end.

The Indonesian cement and concrete complex is in its longest down-cycle in memory. National capacity is 122 Mt against domestic consumption of 66.0 Mt, an oversupply the industry itself puts at close to half of capacity, and the excess has produced an open price war since Chinese groups began adding capacity more than a decade ago [S9]. The consequence for a downstream fabricator is blunt: cement is cheap, which helps its input cost, and finished concrete is cheap, which caps what it can charge. A price war does not spare the fabricator; it squeezes the value added between the two.

Demand is growing, which makes the company’s own decline a share problem rather than a market problem. The national market is forecast to grow by two to three per cent in 2027, supported by the government housing programme, the new capital, the village co-operative building programme, school construction and the nutrition-programme kitchens, with further support from sea-wall, dam and toll-road work [S10][S11]. Indocement reports its own nine-month volumes up around nine per cent year on year, so the market has been expanding while WSBP’s revenue fell [S11][S4]. That divergence is the single most important operating fact in this report.

Regulation matters in two places. Construction services pay final income tax at the reduced rate set under PP No. 9 Tahun 2022, which sits inside the cost base rather than below the line, and that is why the company can report a loss before tax that is also its net loss [S5]. The industry capacity problem is a policy choice: producers have asked the government to maintain the moratorium on new cement plants, an admission that the price war is a supply-policy outcome and not something the participants can fix themselves [S9]. For a fabricator the relevant regulation is public spending: the project pipeline in the 2027 forecasts is government-led, so the demand driver and the payment risk are the same actor.

The competitive landscape has three layers. Cement is an oligopoly of large producers with integrated quarries and kilns. Ready-mix is regional and competitive, with batching plants serving a transport radius. Precast fabrication is project-by-project and fragmented, with a handful of state-linked fabricators, contractors who self-perform, and Chinese-linked entrants. The company’s position is strongest in the bridge and infrastructure girder niche it was built to serve and weakest wherever the client cares only about price [S5][S9]. It has no pricing power of its own: it bids for work against contractors and suppliers who can also choose to cast in place.

Our five-forces read is unambiguously negative. Buyer power is high and concentrated in a single related group and the state; supplier power is moderate because cement is oversupplied but the company buys at list prices with limited rebate; the threat of new entrants is high in ready-mix and low in structural precast; substitutes are real, since cast-in-situ concrete and steel compete on every design; and rivalry is severe because the whole chain is fighting for volume in a market with excess capacity [S9]. There is no moat to defend. The company’s only durable asset is certification and track record on large public structures, and that is a licence to bid rather than a source of pricing.

External influences run through two commodity links and one macro link. Coal enters through the cement embedded in purchased concrete and through steam curing; diesel, haulage and bitumen enter through project logistics, so Brent is a genuine cost driver and the modelled links reflect that. The LK’s cost note is the anchor for the shares: raw materials were three fifths of FY2025 cost of revenues and factory overhead about an eighth, and the overhead block is where the power and process fuel sit [S5]. The rupiah matters little because revenue and most costs are domestic, but the interest rate matters a great deal because the debt is floating-rate bank money. A high-rate, weak-rupiah, balance-of-payments-pressure regime, which is the macro deck we are given, is close to the worst combination for a levered domestic fabricator with negative free cash flow [S5][S9].

Infrastructure fabrication in Indonesia is politically cyclical. Public works budgets are released late in the year and paid late, so a fabricator typically funds a working-capital peak it then has to collect from a state counterparty. That is why the sector balance sheets carry large receivables, why retention money sits for years, and why suppliers become de facto lenders. It is also why a demand recovery does not automatically repair a fabricator cash flow.

The reported history is a business that halved and then stabilised at the lower level. Revenue was IDR1,971.9bn in FY2024 and IDR1,569.6bn in FY2025, and the nine months to September 2026 came in at 1,078 IDR bn, below the comparable period, in a market that grew [S5][S4][S11]. We model IDR1,448.1bn for the current year, which implies a fourth quarter a few per cent above the run-rate rather than the step-up the company’s plan still requires, and then growth back to IDR1,861.1bn by the end of the forecast as volume returns to the market growth rate and price rises with inflation plus partial cost pass-through.

Margins tell the story of the cycle more clearly than revenue. Gross margin was 18.7% in FY2024 and 17.5% in FY2025, but the nine-month 2026 figures show gross profit of 130 IDR bn on revenue of 1,078 IDR bn, a margin in the low teens, because cement and fuel costs rose into a revenue base that fell [S5][S4]. Our model reproduces that from the actual, not from a haircut: the base margin is the FY2025 actual of 17.5% at FY2025 input costs, and the coal and Brent links take the effective margin to 11.9% this year — which is what the business actually delivered, IDR129.8bn of gross profit on IDR1,077.6bn of revenue in the nine months [S4] — before recovering to 15.6% by FY2031 as ICI4 and Brent fall along the deck path. The recovery is the commodity path, not a pricing assumption: we calibrate pass-through to the realised margin, which implies only about a third of this year’s input-cost step-up is being recovered in prices in the middle of an open price war. We do not use management’s stated margin target: FY2023 gross margin was negative, and a target set in an annual report is not evidence of pricing power [S5][S9].

Operating costs are the second problem. In FY2025 general and administrative expenses were the largest block, followed by selling costs and the charge for non-contributing plant, taking total operating expenses to IDR511.3bn, about a third of revenue [S5]. The company has cut hard, though less than an annual-to-interim comparison suggests: general and administrative costs fell from IDR273.5bn in the first nine months of 2025 to IDR237.8bn in the same period of 2026, about an eighth, and the LK sets a target of a ten per cent reduction against the original budget [S4][S5]. We model the expense ratio falling from 29.0% of revenue this year to 24.0% at the end of the forecast, which is that realised trend plus scale rather than an operating-leverage assumption: in absolute terms IDR446.7bn of cost against IDR419.9bn this year, a broadly flat real cost base on a much larger revenue line.

The data pack materially overstates profitability and we restate it. The pack’s depreciation charge for FY2025 is a fraction of the LK’s IDR152.2bn, and its FY2024 charge is similarly understated against the LK figure; the LK allocates depreciation across cost of revenues, general and administrative expenses and the idle-plant line [S5]. Restating that single line turns reported FY2025 EBITDA into IDR-95.4bn, and it is why our EBITDA is negative where a pack-based screen would show something closer to break-even. We also restate FY2024 EBIT to the LK’s loss before finance cost and tax: the pack’s figure does not reconcile to the reported net loss because it omits the other-expenses line the LK reports, and the LK arithmetic does reconcile [S5].

Finance cost is the claim the operations cannot meet. FY2025 finance cost was IDR289.8bn against EBITDA of IDR-95.4bn, and only 79.7 IDR bn of it was paid in cash, with the balance accrued or capitalised into the restructured instruments [S5]. Interest-bearing debt at the end of September 2026 comprised short-term bank loans, long-term bank loans split between related and third parties, bonds and the mandatory convertible bond of 874 IDR bn, totalling 3,689 IDR bn, against cash of 28.1 IDR bn on the same date [S4][S5]. The FY2025 effective rate was 8.4%, which is the restructured rate rather than a market rate, and the model applies it to opening debt.

The balance sheet is the reason the equity is worth nothing. At the end of September 2026 total liabilities of 5,247 IDR bn exceeded total assets of 2,878 IDR bn, current liabilities exceeded current assets by more than a trillion rupiah, accumulated losses exceeded ten trillion rupiah, and the company’s own note says these conditions indicate material uncertainty that may cast significant doubt on its ability to continue as a going concern [S4]. That is not our characterisation, it is the disclosure in the quarterly accounts, and the tone is harsher than the prior year’s report.

Cash flow confirms it. Cash generated from operations in FY2025 was -27.0 IDR bn, negative before any capital spending, before finance charges and before tax, and the company spent nothing on fixed assets, so free cash flow was negative and has remained so [S5]. Our forecast has free cash flow of IDR-103.7bn this year, improving to IDR-1.8bn at the end of the period but never turning positive, with capex held at maintenance level around one per cent of revenue because there is nothing worth building and no money to build it with. Cash stays positive in our model only because we assume IDR395.0bn of new borrowing this year rising to IDR490.0bn by the end, which in practice means accrued interest, mandatory-convertible-bond accretion and stretched suppliers rather than bank facilities. Debt rises from IDR3,915.4bn to IDR6,070.4bn and equity falls from IDR-2,508.1bn to IDR-5,327.8bn. No plausible financing funds that path other than the conversion mechanism the creditors have already accepted.

Earnings quality, run against the house screen, gives a negative verdict on every measure that applies to a non-financial. The accruals gap is wide: a net loss of IDR-537.4bn against slightly negative operating cash flow means non-cash charges, not cash earnings, are doing the work [S5]. Receivables are concentrated in related parties and aged, and the company’s own plan puts collection at the centre of its liquidity problem [S5][S7]. Related-party revenue is roughly seven tenths of the total and related-party bank debt is a majority of the long-term bank book [S5][S4]. The structure flags are disclosed rather than hidden, which is why we classify them as optics-class and structural rather than manipulation-class, and we found no evidence of fabricated cash or fictitious revenue.

The configured method set for cement is a DCF with EV/EBITDA and P/BV as cross-checks, and only the DCF survives contact with this balance sheet: EV/EBITDA requires positive EBITDA, which WSBP does not have on either the pack or the LK numbers, and P/BV requires positive book equity, which is a deficiency of -2,369 IDR bn [S4][S5]. The engine drops both and renormalises, so we state the weights explicitly rather than pretending a three-method blend exists: DCF at 100%, the other two at nothing. A DCF is also the right primary method for a reason specific to the name: it is the only approach that can price a business whose value is negative before debt, and it therefore makes the claim of the equity transparently worthless rather than hiding the problem behind a multiple of a negative number or a book value that no longer exists.

The cost of capital build is unusual because the balance sheet sets the weights rather than the market. We use a risk-free rate of 7.4%, a default spread of 1.6%, a mature equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%, giving a cost of equity of 21.2% on an unlevered beta of 0.90 levered to 2.30 at a debt-to-equity ratio capped at 2.00; the cap is doing the work, because actual leverage is far beyond any market observation [S4]. With pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% and a tax rate of 22.0%, the weighted average cost of capital is 12.0%. The WACC uses a market cost of debt; the interest forecast uses the 8.4% the LK actually charged on the restructured instruments, because that is the contractual claim rather than a market price. We then apply a liquidity discount of 30.0% because the shares have not traded since the suspension, three-month average daily value traded is negligible and a holder cannot exit at any price in the current state [S2][S0]. That discount is applied on top of a valuation that is already zero, so it changes nothing in the target; it matters only for the record.

The DCF discounts negative free cash flow in every explicit year, and the terminal value is negative too, because a perpetuity growth rate of 2.5% applied to a negative final-year cash flow produces a negative terminal value rather than a rescue. The enterprise value is IDR-125.3bn. We deduct net debt at the 30 September 2026 balance sheet — interest-bearing debt of 3,689 IDR bn less cash of 28.1 IDR bn, which is higher than the IDR3,458.8bn on the last full-year balance sheet because unpaid interest has been added to the debt [S4] — and add back the mandatory convertible bond of 874 IDR bn on the view that it converts into shares rather than being repaid in cash, which is exactly what the current placement is doing [S4][S2]. That produces an equity value of minus several trillion rupiah, which the engine floors at zero under the limited-liability rule: a shareholder cannot owe the company debts. The reported valuation view is therefore Rp0 per share; we publish no target and no expected return against the Rp14 suspension sticker, because neither would be a price an investor could act on.

Cross-checks, where they exist, support the zero. On a liquidation arithmetic, assets of 2,878 IDR bn against liabilities of 5,247 IDR bn leave nothing for equity even before the discount a forced sale of a quarter-utilised precast plant would require [S4]. On a restructured-stub arithmetic, converting the whole debt at the peace-agreement price of 50.81 rupiah would issue about seventy-three billion shares and lift book equity to about ten rupiah a share, below the last traded price of Rp14 — and that price is a VWAP formula written into the settlement rather than a negotiated estimate of value, so it carries no information about what the enterprise is worth [S2]. On an asset-value view, 3.7 Mt of capacity and the associated plant are worth something to the enterprise and nothing to the equity, because the creditors can realise that value without the shareholders’ consent.

The grid is uninformative by construction and we say so rather than dress it up: the limited-liability floor binds in every cell, because the enterprise value is IDR-125.3bn before any debt is subtracted and the unfloored equity value is a negative number several times the last traded price. No plausible discount rate or terminal growth closes a gap of that size, so the table shows the floor, not the sensitivity.

What does today’s price imply? The engine’s reverse DCF cannot be run on this name: the configured target is a revenue-growth input that the volume-price template does not carry, so the solver returns no implied value. The arithmetic can still be stated once, on one basis. The pack capitalises the shares at IDR771.6bn; at the last price of Rp14 on the 56,959 million shares reported at the end of September that figure would be marginally higher, so the pack’s number is the conservative one and we use it throughout. Adding net debt at the September balance sheet gives an enterprise value the business has to justify, and at the engine’s cost of capital and terminal growth that requires a perpetual free cash flow of more than a quarter of last year’s revenue, starting now and growing forever — against a modelled best year, IDR-1.8bn, that is still negative. A buyer at this price is not buying cash flow; he is buying an option on a creditor-funded recapitalisation that leaves existing holders with something.

The dominant risk is liquidity, and it is already manifesting. The eighth coupon on the 2022 bonds, due in September 2026, was deferred for up to ninety days because of liquidity pressure caused by collections coming in below plan, and the company committed to fund it from cash available for debt service within that window [S7]. A failure to pay would put the peace agreement under stress and reopen the restructuring, which is a path to a second haircut for creditors and to nothing at all for shareholders. We rate further deferral as high likelihood and high impact, because it is the mechanism through which the whole capital structure is re-set.

The second risk is the conversion itself, and the direction of the mechanism is worth stating precisely because it is easy to invert. The company is issuing new shares to creditors under the homologated settlement at a conversion price of 50.81 rupiah, far above the last traded price [S2]. Conversion at a higher price issues fewer shares per rupiah of debt extinguished, so this price is the least dilutive version of the mechanism for the existing register, not the most — a conversion struck at the market price would dilute far more. What a high price does not do is create value. Every conversion improves solvency and dilutes the register, but the claim being diluted is already worth nothing, because the enterprise value is negative before the debt is touched; the conversion therefore proves nothing about what the equity is worth, and it is the size of the conversion against the debt, not its price, that determines whether anything is left. On the current documents nothing is. The third risk is operational: a fabricator at roughly a quarter utilisation with a falling order book cannot absorb fixed costs, and the national market’s growth is government-programme dependent, so a budget delay is a revenue delay [S9][S10][S11].

Commodity and macro risk run the other way for the equity. Higher coal and oil raise costs faster than the company can pass them through in a price war, and our model shows the margin compression this year; lower coal and oil help the equity only after the debt is serviced, which it is not. Currency risk is small on the profit and loss because revenue and most costs are domestic, but the floating-rate bank debt makes the interest rate the dominant macro variable, and a higher-for-longer rupiah rate environment adds to a finance cost that already exceeds EBITDA [S4][S5]. Governance risk is covered in the next section; in short, the controlling shareholder is also the largest customer, the largest related-party creditor and the architect of the restructuring, and minority holders have no lever over any of it.

Our scenarios shock the same two drivers by mirrored amounts, because the operations are not where the asymmetry is. In the bear case volume falls by a tenth as the payment schedule slips again and customers delay awards after the coupon deferral, and gross margin gives back two percentage points as material costs rise and price increases do not stick. In the bull case volume is a tenth above base as the state construction programme releases toll, dam and coastal work and WSBP wins external tenders, with gross margin two points better as pass-through holds. The probabilities are 50.0% base, 25.0% bear and 25.0% bull, which reflects a company in a managed restructuring: the most likely path is continuation, not collapse and not recovery. All three scenarios produce the same equity value of Rp0, because the debt arithmetic dominates the operating difference, and we therefore present the table as diagnostic rather than as a probability-weighted view — the weights are the engine’s requirement, not a claim that an operating range this wide discriminates. That is not a modelling failure; it is the finding, because the variable that decides the equity is the capital structure and none of the operating shocks touches it.

So we test the structural cases in words and numbers rather than shock a model that cannot hold them. Convert the whole debt at the peace-agreement price and the share count rises by about seventy-three billion, book equity turns to about ten rupiah a share and the enterprise value is still negative: the most generous conversion case leaves less than today’s price on a book basis and nothing on a cash basis. Set against it, there is a real impairment exposure: the plant is carried at IDR2,015.0bn on a business running at about a quarter of capacity, and related-party trade and retention receivables were IDR289.4bn and IDR134.8bn at the last year-end. A write-down of either would deepen the deficiency and harden the going-concern language, but neither is a cash item, so neither changes the coupon calendar or the runway. What sets the runway is the cash balance of IDR28.1bn at the end of September against the deferred coupon, and that, not the carrying value of the assets, is the binding constraint.

What would change the view, and what we watch as signposts: payment of the deferred coupon inside the ninety-day window rather than a further deferral [S7]; completion and listing of the current placement and the size of the share base afterwards [S2]; full-year revenue against the company’s plan [S5][S6]; the auditor’s opinion and whether the going-concern emphasis is repeated for FY2026 [S4]; and any announcement of a debt write-off or of a conversion large enough against the debt to clear the deficiency. A single signpost is not enough. The view changes when liabilities fall below the value of the assets on a sustainable basis, and nothing in the current disclosure does that.

Ownership is concentrated in the state construction group: Waskita Karya holds 54.3% of the shares and WSBP is described in the press as its listed subsidiary [S0][S2]. The data pack reports a free float of 57.7% of the register, which does not sit easily with a controlling stake of that size and is one reason we treat the float figure as unreliable; more importantly the shares have been suspended since before the current placement, so no float is tradeable in practice [S0][S2]. The board is state-appointed through the group, the restructuring is being executed under a court-homologated peace agreement, and practical authority over the capital structure sits with the creditors and the Ministry of State-Owned Enterprises rather than with the shareholders’ meeting. For a minority holder this is the decisive governance fact: there is no route to influence, and the party that controls the company is also the party the company sells to.

Related-party gravity is unusually high even by Indonesian standards. 1,107 IDR bn of FY2025 revenue came from related parties, related-party trade and retention receivables are large, and long-term bank loans from related parties of more than a trillion rupiah sit on the balance sheet alongside a related-party trade payables book of more than a third of a trillion rupiah [S5][S4]. These are disclosed and priced in the accounts, but they mean the company’s revenue, its receivables quality and a large part of its funding all depend on entities inside the same group and the same state apparatus.

On the audit, the FY2025 financial statements are audited and the going-concern assessment is disclosed; the audit report itself, in the archived PDF, is a scanned image and we could not read the opinion type or the key audit matters, so we do not attribute an opinion to the auditor. That is an open item for this initiation rather than a finding [S5]. The September 2026 quarterly accounts are unaudited, as all interim Indonesian filings are, and they carry the material-uncertainty note verbatim [S4]. There is no dividend and none is possible: the company has an accumulated deficit, negative equity and a contractual cash waterfall, and trailing DPS is zero [S0][S4].

Structure flags, checked against the house screen: repeated private placements converting creditor debt into equity, including the current Stage VII placement [S2]; a mandatory convertible bond that accretes rather than pays [S4]; a PKPU and a homologated peace agreement with a standstill and a cash waterfall [S4]; and a trading suspension [S2]. We found no evidence of pledged controlling shares in the filings we read, no auditor down-tiering, and no fabricated cash or revenue; the flags we did find are disclosed, structural and adverse to minorities rather than fraudulent. On that classification the name is not auto-passed on manipulation grounds, but the structure itself is the reason the equity is valued at zero.

ESG exposure is ordinary for heavy fabrication and secondary to the solvency question. Precast batching and steam curing are energy-intensive and dust-generating, the plants sit near population centres, and the workforce is project-based with the safety exposure that implies; the company discloses a sustainability framework in the annual report, but the material ESG risk for a creditor or shareholder today is the decommissioning and remediation cost of idle plant, which is not quantified [S5]. Governance dominates the ESG score, and it is weak: a distressed state issuer, related-party concentration and a capital structure run for the creditors.

The calendar over the next two quarters is dense and almost entirely about the capital structure. The current placement of new shares to creditors lists in November 2026 and fixes the post-placement share base: 54.3 million shares at a conversion price of 50.81 rupiah, a VWAP formula set by the peace agreement rather than a negotiated valuation, and small against the 3,689 IDR bn of debt — a procedural step, not a price signal [S2]. The ninety-day window on the deferred eighth coupon closes at the end of December 2026; payment, a further deferral or a default are three very different outcomes for the equity, and only the first is consistent with the peace agreement holding [S7]. The next scheduled coupon falls in March 2027 and the full-year 2026 accounts follow, with the auditor’s going-concern judgement the item that matters more than the numbers [S5].

Between now and then we monitor five things, all disclosed monthly or quarterly: revenue against the company’s own plan, since the nine-month run-rate is already behind it [S5][S6]; the gross margin, which is where the coal and oil links show up and where the price war is visible [S4]; cash collections from related parties, the stated cause of the liquidity pressure [S7]; the cash balance against the coupon calendar, because a company with a small cash balance and a deferred coupon has no buffer [S4]; and the size and price of every conversion, because the price runs the other way from the intuition — a conversion at a high price gives the existing register more of the post-conversion equity, not less — and what matters is whether the conversion is large enough to clear the deficiency [S2]. We also track national cement volume growth and the coal and Brent decks, but on our numbers those move the equity value by nothing until the balance sheet is repaired.

bear.narrative: Volume falls 10% as the homologation payment schedule slips again and customers delay awards after the coupon deferral; gross margin gives back 2pp as material costs keep rising and price increases do not stick.

bull.narrative: Volume 10% above base as the Danantara-backed BUMN Karya programme releases toll, dam and coastal work and WSBP wins external tenders; gross margin 2pp better as material-cost pass-through holds.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Volume
assumptions.basis: Tonne-equivalent of precast and ready-mix sold; the company publishes no tonnage, so volume is implied from revenue at the modelled blended price. FY2025 revenue of Rp1.57tn against 3.7Mt of precast capacity implies roughly 0.9-1.0Mt and about a quarter utilisation. 9M-2026 revenue fell 7.8% y/y while the national cement market grew 7.8%, so FY2026E is below FY2025; from FY2027 volume tracks the 2-3% industry growth forecast. [S4][S8][S10][S11]

assumptions.label: Average price
assumptions.basis: Blended revenue per tonne-equivalent: FY2025 revenue of Rp1,569.6bn over roughly 1.0Mt is about Rp1.57m/t. FY2026E follows the 9M-2026 mix, where revenue fell and precast carried the volume; thereafter +3%/yr, roughly IDR inflation plus partial pass-through of material-cost inflation, constrained by 45% national overcapacity and an open price war. [S4][S5][S9]

assumptions.label: Gross margin at FY2025 input costs
assumptions.basis: Set to the FY2025 actual of 17.5% (gross profit Rp274.5bn on revenue Rp1,569.6bn, S5), because the base year must reproduce the last audited accounts at its own input costs; there is no haircut below the actual. The coal and Brent links then do all of the work: with FY2026E ICI4 at 62.0 against 40.56 in FY2025 and Brent at 96.0 against 68.1, and pass-through calibrated to the realised outcome (see link1_pass), the effective margin is the 12.0% actually delivered in the nine months to September 2026 (gross profit Rp129.8bn on revenue Rp1,077.6bn, S4). Recovery to 15.6% by FY2031 follows the deck path for coal and oil, not a volume or price recovery. Management's 20.81% target is not used: FY2023 gross margin was negative and the 2026 revenue target is being missed.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Coal reaches WSBP through steam curing and factory power in the overhead block (Rp172.7bn, 13.3% of FY2025 cost of revenues, S5 note 29) and through the coal embedded in purchased cement inside raw materials (Rp772.1bn, 59.6%). We set the share at 12% of cost of revenues: inside that disclosed envelope, but not the coal-fired kiln exposure a cement producer carries, so the CEMENT house-template value is also the right one for a company that buys its cement. It is the same parameter used for BLES.JK. [S5]

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Calibrated to the last actual rather than to the template: with the FY2025 base at 17.5%, the 12.0% realised gross margin in the nine months to September 2026 (S4) is reproduced when about a third of the modelled coal and oil step-up is recovered in prices. The open price war and the roughly half of national capacity lying idle (S9) are why pass-through is below the template half. [S4][S5][S9]

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Diesel, haulage and bitumen sit in the same overhead block (Rp172.7bn) and in construction services (Rp302.1bn, 23.3% of FY2025 cost of revenues, S5 note 29). We set 8% of cost of revenues, slightly above the BLES.JK 5% because a project fabricator hauls girders and ready-mix to site rather than shipping blocks to distributors. [S5]

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: The same calibration as the coal link: the realised 9M-2026 margin is consistent with about a third of the combined input-cost move being recovered in prices, and most construction contracts are fixed-price so a diesel move inside a project is absorbed. [S4][S5][S9]

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: SG&A, non-contributing plant, final tax and other items over revenue: 29.6% in 9M-2026 (sales 64.4 + G&A 237.8 + non-contributing plant 6.6 + final tax 10.3 on revenue 1,077.6, S4 p.7) and 32.6% in FY2025. The fall to 24% by FY2031 is the realised trend plus scale, not operating leverage: G&A fell 13.0% like-for-like in the nine months (237.8 against 273.5, S4 p.7) and the FY2025 LK targets a further 10% cut against budget (S5); at 24% of FY2031E revenue of 1,861.1 the absolute charge is Rp446.7bn against Rp425.4bn annualised today, so the assumption is a broadly flat real cost base on a revenue line 28% larger.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 9M-2026 depreciation of Rp85.2bn, annualised Rp113.6bn, is 7.8% of modelled FY2026E revenue; FY2025 was Rp152.2bn or 9.7%. It falls as revenue grows against a Rp2.0tn depreciating asset base stated at cost. [S4][S5]

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Maintenance only. FY2025 fixed-asset additions were nil and the company sold Rp4.0bn of assets; 1.2% of revenue is roughly sustaining spend on a Rp2.0tn plant base at about a quarter utilisation. No growth capex. [S5][S8]

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital is negative because payables and customer advances exceed receivables and inventory: Rp-708bn at 30 September 2026 on Rp1,479bn LTM revenue, about -0.48 (S0)(S4). Held flat at -0.46: the company finances itself by stretching suppliers, so working capital scales with activity rather than being paid down.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Final income tax (PPh final) already sits inside opex and the company is loss-making with unrecognised tax losses, so the effective rate on EBIT is nil; 5% is a token rate for any profitable year. [S5]

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance cost of Rp289.8bn on average interest-bearing debt of about Rp3.4tn is 8.4%, the LK's own effective rate on the restructured instruments; only Rp79.7bn was paid in cash and the rest accrued into the mandatory convertible bond and payables. We apply the 8.4% effective rate to opening debt rather than a lower notional coupon. [S5]

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income of Rp2.16bn on average cash of about Rp134bn is 1.6%; balances are small and partly restricted. 3%. [S5]

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The cash deficit is funded by non-payment, not new bank money: FY2025 finance cost was Rp289.8bn of which only Rp79.7bn was paid in cash (S5), and the mandatory convertible bond accreted from Rp727.7bn to Rp807.7bn in FY2025 and Rp874.3bn by 30 September 2026 (S4). The engine has no separate accrual line, so this input carries the whole funding gap: it covers the interest charge at the LK effective rate plus OWK accretion plus the supplier stretch, and it therefore rises with the interest line (Rp296bn in FY2026E to Rp460bn in FY2031E). It is debt-like, so debt rises from Rp3.52tn to about Rp5.9tn by FY2031. No new bank facility is assumed.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 other income/expense was Rp-12.8bn including a Rp7.0bn impairment reversal; we assume nil rather than repeat one-offs. [S5]

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: No minority interests are recognised on the balance sheet. [S5]

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend is possible with an equity deficiency of Rp2.37tn and accumulated losses; trailing DPS is zero. [S0][S4]

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Shares rise through debt-to-equity conversion under the homologation: 56.78bn at end-2025 and 56.96bn at 30 September 2026, plus a further 54.3m shares in November 2026. About 2%/yr is the recent run-rate. [S2][S4]

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Bank Indonesia target range of 2.5% plus or minus 1% for 2026-2027 (S13), the long-run nominal anchor for an IDR revenue base; below the engine cap.

challenges.challenge: The base gross margin is 16.23% (assumptions gross_margin FY2026E 0.1623) but the last actual year delivered 17.49% (274.47/1,569.57, S5), and the basis claims the base is 'measured at FY2025 input costs' — at those same input costs it should be 17.5%, so 1.3pp (about Rp20bn a year of gross profit) is removed with no source. The calibration gate registers the consequence: model EBITDA margin -9.0% against the FY2025A actual -6.1%, a 2.92pp gap (about Rp46bn), and qc_justifications does not address it. On a 17.5% base the links give a 13.4% FY2026 margin against the 12.1% nine-month actual, which is the number that would then need explaining.
challenges.answer: The unsourced 1.3pp haircut is gone: the base gross margin is now the FY2025 actual 17.5% (Rp274.5bn on Rp1,569.6bn, S5) with no downward drift, and pass-through is calibrated so the links reproduce the 12.0% actually realised in 9M-2026 (Rp129.8bn on Rp1,077.6bn, S4). FY2026E now models 11.9%, within 0.15pp of the nine-month actual, so there is no 13.4% margin left to explain. The residual calibration gap (3.2pp, below the 5pp block threshold) is recorded in qc_justifications.calibration.ebitda_margin as the FY2026 input-cost step-up already visible in the LK.

challenges.challenge: Two load-bearing numbers in the prose do not match the model. Section 3 says interest-bearing debt at 30 September 2026 was 'against cash of IDR61.6bn [S4][S5]'; F30 gives Rp28.1bn at 30 September 2026 and Rp61.6bn is the 31 December 2025 column. Section 4 says 'we deduct net debt (IDR3,458.8bn on the last full-year balance sheet)'; the engine deducts Rp3,660.8bn (debt 3,688.9 less cash 28.1, market block). A reader reconciling section 4 to the valuation table is out by Rp202bn and cannot tell which balance-sheet date is used.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now quotes cash at 30 September 2026 (F30, Rp28.1bn, S4) and total interest-bearing debt at the same date (F31, Rp3,688.9bn, S4 note 41 maturity profile). Section 4 deducts net debt at the 30 September 2026 balance sheet - debt F31 less cash F30 - and names the date, with the FY2025 net debt of Rp3,458.8bn shown only as the lower comparator because unpaid interest has been added since. The text and the valuation table now use the same balance-sheet date.

challenges.challenge: The reverse-DCF arithmetic is wrong by about 3.7x and is stated three inconsistent ways. At the engine's WACC of 12.00% and g of 2.5%, EV of 771.6 plus net debt 3,660.8 equals Rp4,432.4bn and needs perpetual FCFF of about Rp411bn, 26% of FY2025 revenue — not 'in the region of the whole of its annual revenue' as section 4 says, and not the 'about Rp726bn ... 46% of FY2025 revenue' in the extreme_call justification. Separately, Rp771.6bn implies Rp13.55 a share: 56.96bn shares at the stated Rp14.00 is Rp797.4bn.
challenges.answer: Recomputed once on the engine's own WACC (12.0%) and g (2.5%): market value Rp771.6bn plus net debt Rp3,660.8bn is Rp4,432.4bn of EV, which needs about Rp421bn of perpetual FCFF from today, 27% of FY2025 revenue - not the whole of revenue. Section 4 and qc_justifications.extreme_call now carry that same figure and both drop the old Rp726bn/46% framing. The Rp771.6bn market value is reconciled in the text: it is the data pack's market block on a lower share count than the 56,959.2m reported at 30 September, so at the last price the pack figure is the marginally conservative one and it is used throughout.

challenges.challenge: The summary names the change case as 'a debt conversion struck near the market price that leaves residual value above the deficiency', but the documented conversion price is Rp50.81 [S2], 3.6x the market, and the report never runs it. At Rp50.81 the Rp3,688.9bn of remaining debt is 72.6bn new shares on today's 56.96bn, and extinguishing it at par turns book equity from -Rp2,368.8bn to about +Rp1,320bn, or Rp10.2 a share. Whether that book is recoverable is the debate; the report asserts zero without doing the arithmetic, and neither the base nor the bull case (volume +10%, margin +2pp) can test it.
challenges.answer: The conversion is now run, not asserted. Full conversion of the remaining debt at the Rp50.81 peace-agreement price (F33, S2) issues about 73bn shares on the 56,959m in issue, lifts book equity from -Rp2,368.8bn to about +Rp1,320bn, or about Rp10.2 a share - below the Rp14 market price - and because the DCF enterprise value is negative before any debt, the equity is still worthless on a cash-flow basis. The report states why the book is not recoverable: an enterprise whose unlevered free cash flow is negative in every forecast year does not support positive equity, so the conversion repairs solvency, not earning power.

challenges.challenge: Section 5 states that 'the equation only improves for existing holders if the conversion price is at or below the market'. That is backwards: conversion at Rp50.81 issues one share per Rp50.81 of debt extinguished, while conversion at Rp14 issues one per Rp14, which is 3.6x more shares for the same debt reduction. A higher conversion price is less dilutive to the existing register, all else equal, and sections 4 and 6 use 'far above the last traded price' as bearish evidence, which is the same inversion.
challenges.answer: The inversion is corrected in sections 4, 5 and 7. Conversion at a higher price issues fewer shares per rupiah of debt extinguished, so the Rp50.81 price is the least dilutive version of the mechanism for the existing register, not the most; a conversion at the market price would dilute roughly 3.6x more. What a high price does not prove is value: the enterprise value is negative before the debt is touched, so the claim being diluted is already worth nothing and the price of the conversion says nothing about the equity.

challenges.challenge: The Rp50.81 conversion price is a formula, not a negotiated valuation: S2 says it 'didapatkan berdasarkan perhitungan volume weighted average price (VWAP) sebagaimana diatur dalam perjanjian perdamaian'. Section 4 says the price 'tells you what the creditors think their own claim is worth' and section 7 calls the placement 'the first hard evidence of how the creditors value their own claim' — the source says it is a mechanical VWAP set by the peace agreement. The placement is also 54,295,065 shares at Rp50.81, Rp2.76bn of debt, 0.075% of the Rp3,688.9bn total, so it cannot be a valuation signal for the other 99.9%.
challenges.answer: The creditor-valuation inference is removed from sections 4 and 7. The text now says the Rp50.81 is a VWAP formula written into the peace agreement (F33, S2), gives the placement size (54.3m shares, F34) and states that Rp2.76bn of debt against Rp3,688.9bn is 0.075% of the total, so it cannot be a valuation signal for the rest of the claim. The restructured-stub cross-check now rests on share count and book equity, not on an inferred creditor price.

challenges.challenge: Four key_inputs are attributed to a source that contains nothing about them: link1_share 0.12, link1_pass 0.50, link2_share 0.08 and link2_pass 0.50 each carry sources [S9]. S9 is a 7,772-character suara.com article on Chinese cement capacity and Indocement pricing; it has no hit for batubara, coal, diesel, solar or biaya energi and says nothing about WSBP's cost structure. The values match the CEMENT peer set (BLES.JK link1 0.12/0.50), so they are house-template parameters — but they drive the FY2026 margin compression and the basis as written cannot be verified. I do not raise this to FATAL only because the parameters are the template's and the target is floored either way.
challenges.answer: All four parameters are re-based. The share of cost exposed now comes from the LK cost note (S5 note 29: raw materials Rp772.1bn, 59.6% of cost of revenues; factory overhead Rp172.7bn, 13.3%; construction services Rp302.1bn, 23.3%) with new facts F37-F39, and the text states the 12%/8% split is the CEMENT house template and the BLES.JK parameter, sitting inside that disclosed envelope rather than assuming kiln exposure. Pass-through is calibrated from the realised 9M-2026 margin, and S9 is cited only for what it contains: the open price war and idle capacity that cap pass-through.

challenges.challenge: The opex drift justification, which is the answer to BLOCK flag drift.opex_pct, compares periods that are not comparable: 'G&A alone fell from Rp380.6bn to Rp237.8bn for the nine months'. Rp380.6bn is the full-year FY2025 charge (S5 page 14, 380,593,521,729); Rp237.8bn is nine months of 2026, and the like-for-like nine months of 2025 is Rp273.5bn (S4 page 7, 273,466,932,349). The fall is 13.0%, not the 37.5% the sentence implies — a 2.9x overstatement used to justify a 5pp fall in opex_pct to 24%.
challenges.answer: The opex justification is restated like-for-like on facts F40/F41: G&A fell from Rp273.5bn to Rp237.8bn across the two nine-month periods, a 13.0% fall, not the 37.5% the annual-to-interim comparison implied. The absolute check is stated: 24% of FY2031E revenue of Rp1,861.1bn is Rp446.7bn against Rp419.9bn in FY2026E, so the path is a broadly flat real cost base on 28% more revenue, which is what justifies the 5.0pp ratio fall. The same numbers now appear in section 3. On the other conservatism point in this checklist item, the cost of debt used for interest is raised from 7.5% to the LK's 8.4% effective rate (S5), and the funding line is raised with it so cash stays positive through the forecast rather than being flattered by a below-market rate.

challenges.challenge: The scenario set is self-declared non-discriminating: 'All three scenarios produce the same equity value of Rp0'. Both shocks (volume 0.9/1.1, gross margin plus or minus 2pp) act on an operating result that is negative before and after, so the 50/25/25 weights carry no information and the bull case cannot test the one variable the thesis depends on, which is the capital structure. The mirrored-shock requirement is met; the analytical purpose is not.
challenges.answer: The scenario table is relabelled diagnostic in section 5: the weights stay because the engine requires them, but the text says they carry no information because the floor binds in all three cases, and the variable that decides the equity is the capital structure. A structural case is added in prose - full conversion at Rp50.81, book equity about Rp10.2 a share and negative EV; full write-off of the related-party receivable book and half the plant, both non-cash; and the coupon calendar against the Rp28.1bn cash balance - and its value is stated rather than left to operating shocks.

challenges.challenge: No impairment is modelled in any scenario although the assets support one: net carrying value of property, plant and equipment was Rp2,100.2bn at 30 September 2026 (S4 pages 84-85) on a business at 21-25% utilisation, and related-party receivables at 31 December 2025 were Rp514.2bn (trade 289.4 plus retention 134.8 plus gross amounts due from customers 90.1, S5 page 12), 33% of revenue. The nine-month 2026 recoverable-amount review produced only a Rp617m net reversal, and the report never quantifies what a write-down does to the deficiency or to the coupon calendar.
challenges.answer: The exposure is now sized with facts, and one date is corrected: net PP&E was Rp2,015.0bn at 30 September 2026 (F32, S4 p.5); the Rp2,100.2bn the review cites is the 31 December 2025 comparative column. Related-party trade and retention receivables were Rp289.4bn (F35) and Rp134.8bn (F36) at that year-end. Section 5 puts both in the bear discussion and states the key point: neither is a cash item, so an impairment deepens the deficiency and hardens the going-concern wording but does not move the coupon calendar or the runway, which is set by the Rp28.1bn cash balance. The 9M-2026 review produced only a marginal net reversal, so carrying value is supported on the company's own test but remains a book judgement.

challenges.challenge: Section 2 says 'the largest producer reports its own nine-month volumes up around nine per cent year on year [S11]'. S11 attributes the 15.75Mt and +9% to Indocement, while the industry's largest producer by capacity is Semen Indonesia. The load-bearing divergence number, the national market at +7.8% to Q3-2026 on ASI data, is correctly sourced and stands.
challenges.answer: Section 2 now names Indocement as the producer reporting nine-month volumes up around nine per cent (S11). The national market at +7.8% to Q3-2026 on ASI data, which was already sourced, stands as the load-bearing divergence number.

challenges.challenge: Section 1 says the Rp2,100bn 2026 revenue plan 'implies a weaker final quarter than the run-rate'. With nine-month revenue of Rp1,077.6bn the plan requires fourth-quarter revenue of Rp1,022.4bn, which is 2.85x the quarterly run-rate of Rp358.9bn: the plan is missed by about 31%, not by a weak quarter. The model's own FY2026E implies fourth-quarter revenue of Rp370.5bn, 3.1% above the run-rate, so 'no better than the run-rate' misdescribes the model as well.
challenges.answer: Section 1 now states the plan's implication correctly: against the Rp2,100bn target and Rp1,077.6bn of nine-month revenue (F14, F21), the implied final quarter is roughly the size of the entire first nine months, about three times the quarterly run-rate, so the plan is missed by close to a third. The description of FY2026E is aligned with the engine: it implies a fourth quarter a few per cent above the run-rate, not 'no better than the run-rate'. The same correction is made in section 3.

challenges.challenge: The WACC and terminal-growth sensitivity grid is five by five zeros because the equity value is floored at zero, so the table tells a reader nothing about how far below zero the model sits. The unfloored DCF equity value is Rp-3,115.2bn, or Rp-54.69 a share (model value_unfloored -54.691).
challenges.answer: Section 4 now says the grid is uninformative by construction rather than printing a page of zeros without comment: the floor binds in every cell, the enterprise value is negative before debt (IDR-125.3bn), and the unfloored equity value is a negative number several times the last traded price. The margin of insolvency is therefore visible at the enterprise level and in words at the equity level, because the renderer exposes no placeholder for value_unfloored.

challenges.challenge: A suspended line is rated rather than NOT RATED. WSBP shares remain suspended at the last print of Rp14 (S2, 11 Nov 2026, verbatim: 'perdagangan saham ... masih dihentikan sementara (suspended) dan terakhir kali dibanderol Rp14 per saham'; the assumptions post-balance-sheet note records the same), yet the model publishes SELL, a Rp0 target and a -100.0% expected return against that Rp14 sticker, because coverage/universe/idx_master.csv still records status 'listed' and fund record only forces NOT RATED from the master status (lines 1167-1170). fund rules coverage.ratings reserves suspended lines for NOT RATED, and the house publishes PLIN, BOSS and ZBRA as NOT RATED valuation views; SMCB was corrected on this exact defect earlier today. The report is internally inconsistent with itself: section 6 states the shares 'have been suspended since before the current placement' and section 4 applies a 30% liquidity discount because 'the shares have not traded since the suspension'.
challenges.answer: Set WSBP.JK to suspended in fund record (matching the SMCB row) and re-ran the engine so the rating prints NOT RATED; republished the zero as a valuation view with no target and no expected return, removing the Rp14 return arithmetic [S2]

missing_bull_case.note: The one upside that can move the equity off zero, the documented Rp50.81 debt conversion, is named in the summary but never modelled; the bull case adds 10% volume and 2pp of margin to a business whose EBITDA is negative in every year.

missing_bear_case.note: No impairment of the Rp2.10tn plant (21-25% utilisation) or of Rp514bn of related-party receivables, and no second-restructuring cash-runway stress; the coupon deferral is described but never put through the model.

assumption_realism.note: Volume, price and the coal/oil deck path are anchored to sourced facts and match the CEMENT peer set, but the 16.23% gross-margin base sits 1.3pp under the last actual with no source, and the opex path rests on a mis-periodised comparison.

evidence_and_citations.note: Most facts reproduce verbatim (F1-F5, F8-F13, F16-F25, F28-F30 all checked), but four coal/oil link parameters cite S9, which contains no cost data, and the Rp50.81 conversion price is a VWAP formula read as a creditor valuation.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF-only is the correct call (no positive EBITDA or book equity) and the bridge, limited-liability floor and cost-of-capital build are sound; but the prose misstates cash and net debt, the reverse-DCF arithmetic is 3.7x off, and the sensitivity table is all zeros.

flags.message: a.opex_pct moves -5.0pp from FY2026E to FY2031E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: opex_pct falls 5.0pp because the cost base is already shrinking, not because of operating leverage: total operating expenses were 32.6% of FY2025 revenue but 29.6% in 9M-2026, and G&A fell 13.0% like-for-like, to Rp237.8bn from Rp273.5bn for the nine months (S4 p.7); the FY2025 LK targets a further 10% cut against the original budget (S5). At 24% of FY2031E revenue the absolute charge is Rp446.7bn against Rp425.4bn annualised today, so the path is a flat real cost base on a revenue line 28% larger, not a margin recovery. [S4][S5]

flags.message: ebit FY2024A restated at 2.10x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The pack omits Rp376.7bn of other expenses: its FY2024 EBIT of Rp-339.4bn less its own finance cost of Rp203.2bn implies a Rp-542.5bn pre-tax loss, but the LK reports a Rp-997.3bn net loss. The LK line RUGI SEBELUM BEBAN KEUANGAN DAN PAJAK of Rp-713.4bn less finance cost of Rp283.9bn reconciles exactly to the reported net loss, so we model the LK figure. [S5]

flags.message: expected return -100%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers. First, EBITDA is negative even after restating D&A to the LK charge of Rp152.2bn (Rp-95.4bn in FY2025) while finance cost is Rp289.8bn and only Rp79.7bn of it was paid in cash [S5]. Second, liabilities of Rp5,247.1bn exceed assets of Rp2,878.3bn at 30 September 2026, a Rp2,368.8bn deficiency, with the going-concern note flagging material uncertainty and the eighth bond coupon deferred by up to 90 days [S4][S7]. Third, the DCF enterprise value is Rp-125.3bn before any debt, so the equity is Rp-2,910.4bn unfloored (Rp-51.10 a share) and zero under limited liability. What the price implies: the pack market value of Rp771.6bn plus net debt of Rp3,660.8bn (interest-bearing debt 3,688.9 less cash 28.1 at 30 September 2026) is Rp4,432.4bn of enterprise value, which at the engine 12.0% WACC and 2.5% growth needs about Rp421bn of perpetual FCFF from today, 27% of FY2025 revenue, against a modelled best year of Rp-1.8bn. The configured reverse-DCF target is revenue growth, which the volume-price template does not carry, so the engine returns no implied value and we state the arithmetic instead [S2][S4].
